newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bonn coalition sets tax bill, funding drive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonn coalition sets tax bill, funding drive.

text.p: Germany's coalition government on Tuesday approved Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1998 tax bill and rubber-stamped plans to throw billions of marks in cheap financing at the country's stricken building industry.
The tax bill would introduce the first phase of a two-stage plan to slash 30 billion marks ($17.7 billion) in taxes by making initial cuts in corporate and commercial tax rates.

"The 1998 tax bill will strengthen forces for growth," Waigel said after a cabinet meeting. "No smart investor should miss out on unparallelled write-off rates to invest now and pay lower taxes on the resulting profits later."

Cutting the main corporation tax rate to 40 percent from 45 percent, and unifying it with the commercial income tax rate, now 47 percent, would be offset next year mainly by tightening up on opportunities to write off investment costs.
The bill would also cut the solidarity surcharge -- raised to finance aid to east Germany -- by two points to 5.5 percent, lightening the tax load by 7.5 billion marks.

Waigel was making good on a warning he had made that he would go ahead and legislate if the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) do not return to cross-party tax negotiations they broke off in a clash last week over cutting coal subsidies.
The SPD said it had told the government it would be putting its conditions for restarting talks in writing to Chancellor Helmut Kohl before deciding whether to rejoin the talks.
"Whether there will be more talks...will depend on the Chancellor's answer," SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said.
Waigel said he would respond on Wednesday to the SPD's note, and added he was certain there would be more talks. "We'll see what happens after Easter," he told reporters.

With the tax talks in limbo, the three coalition parties were expected to agree to introduce Waigel's tax bill to parliament on Friday. There, deadlock could drag through this year because the SPD has blocking control of the upper house.
In a bid to boost job creation to fight record post-war unemployment of 4.7 million, Kohl's cabinet also cleared a 25 billion mark programme aimed at boosting the building industry.

Of the total, 20 billion marks would be provided as cheap loans by the Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau development agency and the Deutsche Ausgleichsbank. The rest will be made available through privately-funded public works projects.
All the funding will be off-budget and have no impact on Waigel's bid to cut the budget deficit below three percent of GDP this year to qualify for European monetary union in 1999.

The measures, combined with the tax bill and draft measures already revealed to cut corporate taxes again and slash income tax in 1999, were hailed by the government as a concentrated effort to boost jobs and the economy.
"Never before have so many decisive measures been taken in such a short time to boost investment," Waigel and Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said in a joint statement.

Coalition leaders pinned the blame for the breakdown of the tax talks on SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine. "We want to fight unemployment, but Lafontaine just wants personal power," said Joachim Hoerster, Christian Democrat (CDU/CSU) chief whip.
Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said: "Lafontaine wants to let the talks collapse."
